Ana Ferreira did not touch an oar until she was seventeen [s:federation]. Before that she swam. Badly, by her own account, and mostly to please a coach who thought her long arms were wasted on the pool [s:daily].

## Early life in Porto

She grew up close to the Douro. The river is wide there, brown after rain and crowded with tourist boats in summer. A school friend took her to a club open day in 2011. She stayed for the free lunch, then for the boats. Within a year the club had moved her from a heavy training quad into a single scull, which is unusual for a beginner and says something about how fast she was learning [s:federation].

Her parents were not sporting people. Her father drove a delivery van; her mother worked nights at a hospital. Training started at six in the morning, so for two years the van doubled as her lift to the river.

## Career

Her first international race was a disaster. She caught a crab in the opening strokes, nearly went in, and finished last. The interview she gave afterwards was short and blunt: she would be back, and she would be faster [s:daily]. She was. Three seasons later she won a national title, and in 2021 a world title in the lightweight single, beating a field that included two previous champions [s:federation].

What changed? Coaches point to her start. She had always finished strongly, but she lost too much ground in the first 500 metres. A winter spent on short, ugly sprint pieces fixed that.

## Injury and return

A rib stress fracture cost her most of 2023. Rowers get these more often than people think, because the same muscles pull on the ribs thousands of times a session. She has said the hardest part was not the pain but watching races on a laptop [s:daily]. She returned in 2024 and placed fourth at the European championships, which she called a good result and a bad day.

## Style and reputation

Ferreira rows with an unusually long finish and a quiet, almost lazy recovery. Commentators like to say she makes it look easy. It is not easy, and she will tell you so.
